title: AVL Trees: Maintain Order and Balance
summary: Follow pointer changes, maintain height metadata, and prove that local repair gives logarithmic ordered operations.
objectives: Validate ordering, stored height and balance independently

sections.title: Why balanced order matters
sections.body: A BST keeps smaller keys on the left and larger keys on the right. This supports predecessor, successor and sorted traversal, unlike an unordered hash map. But inserting sorted keys into a plain BST makes a chain, so search and updates become linear. AVL trees impose a local height constraint that prevents this degeneration while retaining ordered operations.

sections.title: Terminology and representation
sections.body: A root has no parent; leaves have no children. A subtree contains a node and all its descendants. Depth counts edges from the root; height describes the longest downward path. This lesson uses height(empty)=0 and height(leaf)=1, a node-count convention. Each node stores key, left child, right child and height. The implementation represents a set: duplicate inserts do nothing. A multiset needs an explicit count field or a consistent tie-breaking key.

sections.title: Three invariants, not one
sections.body: Every left-subtree key is smaller than the node key; every right-subtree key is larger. Stored height equals 1+max(height(left),height(right)). Balance factor is height(left)-height(right) and must be -1, 0 or 1 at every node after an operation. A visually symmetric tree can still have incorrect height metadata; check all three invariants independently.

sections.title: Rotations preserve the search order
sections.body: For a right rotation at y, let x=y.left and B=x.right. Promote x, attach y as x.right, and move B to y.left. Before and after, the inorder sequence is A,x,B,y,C. Therefore keys remain ordered. No keys are allocated or removed by a rotation; only links and heights change. Update the demoted node y before promoted node x, because the latter height depends on the former. Return the new subtree root so the caller can reconnect it.

sections.title: LL, RR, LR and RL
sections.body: If a node has balance +2 and its left child has nonnegative balance, use one right rotation (LL repair). If the left child is right-heavy, first rotate that child left, then rotate the node right (LR repair). Mirror these for balance -2: RR uses a left rotation, RL rotates the right child right before rotating the node left. The labels describe heavy paths, not rotation direction. Sequences [30,20,10], [10,20,30], [30,10,20], [10,30,20] isolate the four insertion cases.

sections.title: Insertion and return-path repair
sections.body: Descend by the BST comparison until an empty link, allocate a leaf, and return toward the root. At each ancestor first reconnect the returned child, recompute height, inspect balance and rotate if necessary. The insertion affects only one search path. Rebalancing the first unbalanced ancestor restores its previous subtree height, so insertion needs at most one single or double rotation, though metadata traversal still visits O(log n) ancestors. The generic recursive code safely checks all ancestors.

sections.title: Deletion requires its own reasoning
sections.body: Delete a leaf by returning an empty link. Delete a node with one child by returning that child. With two children, copy the inorder successor key from the right subtree’s minimum and recursively delete that successor. Then recompute heights and rebalance while returning to the root. Deletion may shrink a repaired subtree and trigger imbalance higher up, so repairs can cascade through O(log n) ancestors. Determine repair cases from child balance, not the deleted key. In deletion the heavy child can have balance zero: a single rotation is still appropriate.

sections.title: Search, extrema and neighbors
sections.body: Search follows comparisons from the root and stops at an equal key or empty link. Minimum follows left links; maximum follows right links. To find a successor, use the right subtree minimum when a right child exists; otherwise the successor is the lowest ancestor for which the searched key lies in its left subtree. Without parent pointers, keep that ancestor candidate during a root-to-key search. Predecessor is symmetric. Inorder traversal yields sorted keys in Θ(n) time, with O(log n) recursive stack in a valid AVL tree.

sections.title: Why height stays logarithmic
sections.body: Let N(h) be the fewest nodes in an AVL tree of height h. N(0)=0, N(1)=1, and N(h)=1+N(h-1)+N(h-2): to minimize nodes, child heights differ by one. This Fibonacci-like recurrence grows exponentially with h, so h=O(log n). Separately, rotations preserve inorder order and fix local height imbalance. Structural induction along the update path shows repaired subtrees retain BST order, accurate heights and balance. The height argument then bounds future operations.

sections.title: Memory view and ownership
sections.body: Nodes are usually separate heap allocations, with child references or pointers and height metadata. Searches chase dependent pointers and may miss cache lines, unlike contiguous array scans. Recursive updates occupy O(log n) call frames. The C++ sample owns nodes through the root, deletes removed nodes and destroys the remaining tree at the end; do not copy its raw owning root as though it were an independent container. Production C++ containers should make ownership and exception behavior explicit. Managed runtimes reclaim unreachable nodes, but that does not remove allocation or locality costs.

sections.title: Edge cases and debugging
sections.body: Delete an absent key, delete the root repeatedly, insert duplicate keys, and exercise deletion when a heavy child has balance zero. A useful validator recursively returns actual height while checking ordering bounds and absolute child-height difference. Test the whole tree after every operation rather than only the root balance. The commonest pointer bug is failing to assign root=insert(root,key) or root=erase(root,key), which loses a rotation at the root.

sections.title: AVL, ordinary BST and Red-Black Tree
sections.body: An ordinary BST may have linear height. AVL and Red-Black trees both offer logarithmic worst-case ordered operations, using different balance invariants. AVL constrains heights more tightly; Red-Black trees permit a looser shape and use color repair. Actual lookup/update tradeoffs depend on layout, allocation and workload, so compare measurements rather than promising one always wins. B-trees optimize branching and page locality; hash tables are attractive for unordered membership but do not provide sorted traversal or neighboring-key queries.

sections.title: Exercises that test understanding
sections.body: Predict the promoted root for all four three-key sequences before playing the trace. Draw the middle subtree that changes parent during a rotation. Insert 4,2,6,1,3,5,7, then delete keys in ascending order and check every ancestor. Extend the node with subtree size and update it during rotations to support rank and selection. Finally explain why deletion repair cannot be selected solely from the deleted key.

sections.title: Historical and advanced connections
sections.body: AVL is named for Adelson-Velsky and Landis. The essential idea is an ordered tree whose local metadata controls global height. That idea leads to augmented balanced trees, interval indexes and order-statistic sets. Persistent versions copy the modified search path instead of mutating shared nodes; concurrent versions must coordinate pointer publication and reclamation as well as ordering. Those are additional engineering problems, not consequences automatically solved by balancing.

pseudocode:
update subtree using BST rules
reconnect changed child
recompute height
if left-heavy: optionally rotate left child, then rotate right
if right-heavy: optionally rotate right child, then rotate left
return new subtree root

complexity.why: The AVL recurrence bounds height; repair uses constant work per ancestor.
A fixed number of links and height fields change.
Each node is visited once; recursion follows balanced height.

options: Left rotation at 10 then right at 30
quiz.explanation: The left child is right-heavy, so this is an LR case.

quiz.prompt: During a right rotation, whose height must be updated first?
quiz.explanation: The promoted node depends on the demoted node’s new height.

quiz.prompt: Why can deletion require repairs at several ancestors?
options: A repaired subtree can become shorter

quiz.prompt: What recurrence bounds minimum nodes at height h?
quiz.explanation: The sparsest allowed children differ in height by one.

problems.title: Validate balance from actual structure
problems.statement: Implement isBalanced(root) / is_balanced(root). Nodes have left and right fields; do not trust a stored height. Return whether every node has child heights differing by at most one. An empty tree is balanced. This checks balance only, not BST ordering.
problems.constraints: Tree is acyclic; at most 1000 nodes; O(n) time required.
examples: Three nodes chained through left links → false
Root with two leaf children → true
hints: A subtree result can report both its height and whether it is valid.
Use a negative sentinel for imbalance.
Compute each subtree once, then compare the returned heights.

solution.naive: Recompute subtree height independently at every node, costing O(n²) on a chain.
solution.insight: Return the height while validating the same subtree.
solution.algorithm: Postorder recursion returns -1 on imbalance, otherwise 1+max(left,right).
solution.correctness: By structural induction, each valid return is the actual height and each invalid return witnesses an unbalanced descendant.
